title: Love and awe (Yesodei HaTorah 2:2)
hook: contemplating the wonders of creation leads to love and awe

segments.voice: Yesterday, the opening sentence of the code, and your line: foundation of foundations. What did you lean on, and what was it resting on? Day one thousand one hundred forty-four.

The Torah commands love. "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart." It also commands awe, or fear. But a feeling is a strange thing to command. Nobody can be ordered into loving someone. So Maimonides asks the obvious question, right there in his code, in the second chapter: what is the way to love God, and to stand in awe? His answer doesn't begin with a prayer or a rule. It begins with looking at the world.
screen: `THE TORAH COMMANDS LOVE.` → `CAN A FEELING BE COMMANDED?` → `HIS ANSWER: LOOK.`

segments.voice: Love and awe. In Hebrew, ahavah and yirah. Here is his answer, in plain English. When a person thinks carefully about God's great and wondrous works and creatures, and sees in them a wisdom with no measure and no end, that person at once loves, and praises, and longs to know. Turn it four ways. First, the road in. Love isn't produced by willpower. It comes from attention. Look closely enough at how a thing is made, and something in you moves toward its maker. Maimonides says the person thirsts, and he borrows a line from the Psalms: "My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God." Second, the turn. Keep looking, he says, and the same thoughts bring a person up short. You step back. You realize how small you are, a creature with a little knowledge, standing before a wisdom without limit. That stepping back is awe. And again he reaches for a psalm: "What is man, that Thou art mindful of him?" Third, the pairing. These aren't two separate exercises. One act of attention produces both. Love draws you closer. Awe makes you step back. Maimonides holds them together, like breathing in and breathing out. Fourth, what comes next. Right after this, his code describes the structure of the world as the science of his day understood it, the spheres, the stars, the elements. Some of that science has not lasted. But the method has: learn how the world works, and let what you learn lead to wonder. For Maimonides, studying creation isn't a distraction from the religious life. It is one of its doors.
screen: `AHAVAH AND YIRAH.` · `ATTENTION LEADS TO LOVE.` · `THEN YOU STEP BACK: AWE.` · `ONE LOOK, TWO MOVEMENTS.` · then, large: `MY SOUL THIRSTETH FOR GOD.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to look closely at one natural thing. A leaf. A stone. Your own hand. A cloud through the window. Settle, and let your breath slow. Look at it as if you'd never seen one before. Its edges. Its lines. How it's put together. Let the looking run long. Notice if something moves toward it, a little warmth, a little delight. Then notice the other movement, the step back, how much about it you don't know. Let both be there. The bell holds the time.
Love and awe. Ahavah and yirah: for Maimonides, the two movements that come from looking closely at creation, drawing near and standing back. Today's word.
Your line: love and awe. Today, once, stop and look properly at something alive, a tree, a bird, a face, long enough to feel both. Day one thousand one hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Jews who study Maimonides read Yesodei HaTorah 2:2 as a guide to the commandments to love and to fear God, and some take it as a reason to study the natural world as part of a religious life.

fork.setup: the Torah commands you to love God. you can't order yourself to feel something. what does Maimonides say to do?
options: repeat the command until the feeling comes.
look closely at creation and see its wisdom.
wait until love arrives on its own.
fork.reveal: he says contemplating God's great and wondrous works leads straight to love, and then, as you keep looking, to awe.

original.note: Hebrew: love and awe (or fear), the pair Maimonides joins in Yesodei HaTorah 2:2.

trapdoor: what you thought: love of God is a feeling you either have or don't.
what it means: for Maimonides, careful attention to creation produces love, and then awe.
what a scholar hears: ahavah and yirah as one act of contemplation with two movements, and the study of nature as a commanded path toward God.

notes: Yesodei HaTorah 2:2 paraphrased; Maimonides cites Psalm 42:3 and Psalm 8:4–5 there. Please confirm JPS 1917 verse numbers and wording (KJV has the same wording at 42:2 and 8:4).
